https://www.heraldscotland.com/news/2629.text: Ryanair warns Edinburgh Airport passengers of EES queues Edinburgh Airport Ryanair Leisure Travel By Katie Collier Trending News Reporter Share 0 Comments Ryanair has warned everyone travelling from Edinburgh Airport to be aware of the long EES queues at 16 European airports this summer (Image: Getty) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Ryanair has issued a warning to Brits flying from Edinburgh Airport to Europe this summer, saying passengers should be prepared for "significant" queues at 16 major airports. The disruption, which is affecting 16 airports (all of which Edinburgh flies to), is linked to the European Union’s Entry Exit System (EES), which has continued to cause delays months after its introduction. First launched in October last year, the rollout accelerated on April 10. The system now requires British travellers and other non-EU visitors to provide biometric data, including fingerprints and facial scans, when entering the Schengen Area. The new EES has received significant backlash since its introduction, with it causing long waits for passengers at airports. Some travellers have already experienced waits of up to six hours, and industry experts warn these disruptions could continue for up to two years. Major airlines, including Jet2 and Ryanair, have called for the rollout of the new system to be suspended until after the summer to allow for a "smoother airport experience" during peak travel season. CEO of Malta Air, David O’Brien, even threatened to pull all flights to Malta due to the extended wait times caused by the EES at airports. EES to cause long queues at 16 major airports this summer Brits heading to Europe this summer have been told to expect more delays due to the EES. Ryanair has outlined 16 European airports where travellers can expect "significant" queues, which you can travel to from Edinburgh Airport: Tenerife South Palma/Majorca Alicante Malaga Milan Bergamo Milan Malpensa Krakow Paris Beauvais Lisbon Madrid Lanzarote Verona Berlin Cologne Frankfurt Hahn Budapest Chief operations officer at Ryanair, Neal McMahon, said: "Families heading away for a well-earned summer holiday should be thinking about suitcases, suncream and sangria, not standing in passport queues for hours. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Edinburgh Airport (@edinburghairport) "The reality is that the EES system isn’t working properly and families are paying the price for a system that does not work months after launch. "Passengers should not be the testing ground for unfished border infrastructure." Mr McMahon has backed calls from EU Member States to extend current EES flexibilities into early 2027. This extension would give airports and border authorities more time to fix malfunctioning kiosks, increase staffing levels, and ensure the system can operate efficiently before full enforcement is introduced. He said: "We support calls from EU Member States to urgently extend the EES flexibilities. "This will give airports and border authorities the time to improve the infrastructure, fix the broken devices and hire more staff so that families can travel through Europe without disruption." Ryanair has advised UK passengers travelling to and from non-Schengen destinations, or transiting through affected European airports, to allow extra time for their journey and be prepared for lengthy waits at passport control. What you need to apply for ETIAS ETIAS launch delayed until 2027 Meanwhile, the launch of the EU's new European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS) has been delayed until 2027. The ETIAS is a pre-authorisation scheme which will apply to UK passport holders and other visa-exempt travellers entering 30 European countries for short stays. Applicants will be required to pay a €20 fee, though travellers under 18 or over 70 will be exempt. The ETIAS was expected to launch later this year, but it has now been delayed until 2027, according to the Financial Times. The decision is due to "technical glitches" and delays with the EES, which only recently came online after being postponed from 2022. EU home affairs commissioner, Magnus Brunner, said the delays were due to "other factors", including insufficient staff or lack of adequate infrastructure. EU-Lisa, the agency responsible for ETIAS, has reportedly acknowledged that "launching it by the end of this year as planned was no longer feasible". Recommended reading: Edinburgh Airport passengers warned rule change could see them denied entry to Spain Edinburgh Airport passengers warned of 6-hour airport queues in this holiday hotspot Edinburgh Airport passengers warned of six-hour queues at four holiday hotspots The European Commission will set the official launch date only after EU-Lisa confirms the system has been fully tested and is ready. A commission spokesperson said: "Preparations for the launch of ETIAS are ongoing. "Obviously, as with any large-scale IT system, many factors come into play when deciding when to launch it." http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/20/russi.text: Petrol was available at fewer than three in 10 petrol stations across Russia on Wednesday, the latest sign that a second wave of fuel shortages is hitting harder than the first, with queues forming at pumps in Moscow for the first time.The monitoring app Gdebenz put nationwide petrol availability at 28% of filling stations on Wednesday, down from 41% a week earlier.Fuel restrictions — including limits on the volume sold per customer, QR-based rationing and odd-even number plate schemes — were in place in nearly all regions as of last Saturday, according to Benzinmap, which tracks restrictions and prices nationwide.Gazprom Neft filling stations in Moscow set a temporary cap of 40 litres per fill-up. Tatneft capped petrol at 50 litres and diesel at 60. By Wednesday, the Yandex Fuel service showed AI-92 petrol available at just one in 10 stations in the capital.The crisis is the direct result of Kyiv's sustained drone campaign against Russian oil infrastructure in a bid to weaken its war machine amid Moscow's ongoing all-out invasion of Ukraine. By early July every major refinery in Russia had been struck at least once.In the first two weeks of August alone, nearly a dozen more facilities were hit, including Yaroslavnefteorgsintez in Yaroslavl, two refineries in Bashkortostan and export infrastructure at the port of Ust-Luga.Russian Forbes calculated that damaged refineries now account for 54% of total national refining capacity. Daily petrol output fell to between 75,000 and 80,000 tonnes in July, against summer demand of 115,000 to 120,000 tonnes — a daily deficit of roughly 35%.Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged the shortage at the end of July, describing it as "non-critical". He repeated the phrase on Wednesday."There are no critical consequences from such attacks, there have been none and there cannot be any. But they do, of course, cause us damage; that is obvious, we understand it, we see it and we know it," Putin said.Disagreements over imports further the crisisRussia's position as one of the world's largest oil exporters has not shielded it from the shortages.In July Moscow banned petrol and diesel exports to protect domestic supply. It has been importing fuel by rail from Belarus — shipments that surged 25-fold year on year between January and July — Kazakhstan and for the first time Morocco, when a Lukoil-supplied cargo of approximately 30,000 tonnes of AI-92 was loaded at Tangier and shipped to Murmansk.Much of the imported fuel has not reached consumers: according to Russian industry sources cited by the portal InfoTEK, large volumes of Indian and Moroccan petrol are stuck at Murmansk because suppliers want between 110,000 and 130,000 roubles per tonne, while the state regulator is demanding a price below 78,000 roubles.A further supply gap is expected in September when Belarus's Novopolotsk refinery undergoes scheduled maintenance.Belarus supplied a record 212,000 tonnes of petrol and 162,000 tonnes of diesel to Russia in July. It now processes Russian crude on a tolling basis and is Moscow's most important external fuel source. Both of Belarus' refineries — Novopolotsk and Mozyr — have a combined export capacity of roughly 2 million tonnes per year, a fraction of what Russia needs.Retail petrol prices rose 7.4% in the first half of 2026 to an average of 70 roubles per litre, and diesel by more than 12%, according to official data. Residents in some regions say prices have exceeded 100 roubles per litre (€1.02).The Kremlin has ordered the Federal Antimonopoly Service to tighten price controls; the agency said on Wednesday it had opened 41 cases against oil companies for violations.The crisis has forced Russia to reintroduce fuel grades that it banned in the 2010s. On 5 August the government authorised the production, import and sale of Euro-2, Euro-3 and Euro-4 petrol for almost a year.High-sulphur fuel below the Euro-5 standard can degrade modern engines and produces significantly higher levels of air pollutants. Trading in the lower grades started on the St Petersburg exchange on Tuesday.Meanwhile, authorities are prosecuting people who have complained publicly about the shortages.In Volgograd, authorities detained five residents after they recorded a video message to the head of the Russian Investigative Committee Alexander Bastrykin, complaining that officials filled up without restrictions while ordinary drivers faced rationing.One received five days' administrative arrest, while another was fined. A Perm resident who staged a solo picket over petrol access was also fined.

https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/.text: Philstar.com HOME Headlines Opinion Nation World Business Sports Entertainment Lifestyle Events Other Sections The Philippine Star Pilipino Star Ngayon HOME Bansa Metro Probinsiya Opinyon Palaro Showbiz True Confessions Dr. Love Litra-talk Kutob Komiks The Freeman HOME Cebu News Opinion Metro Cebu Region Cebu Business Cebu Sports Cebu Lifestyle Cebu Entertainment Pang-Masa HOME Police Metro Punto Mo Pang Movies PM Sports Para Manalo Para Malibang Banat HOME Balita Opinyon Kalingawan Showbiz Palaro Imong Kapalaran Punsoy Interaksyon HOME Trends + Spotlights Politics + Issues Celebrities Hobbies + Interests Rumor Cop Coupons HOME Top Stores Offers By Category Latest Posts SARA ON TRIAL INFO DISORDER SONA 2026 DUTERTE AT ICC FUEL PRICE TRACKER EXPLAINERS FACT CHECKS ENVIRONMENT My Profile Sign Out HOME HEADLINES OPINION NATION WORLD BUSINESS SPORTS ENTERTAINMENT LIFESTYLE EVENTS COUPONS OTHER SECTIONS Headlines Philippines, Poland ink mutual legal assistance pact MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines and Poland yesterday signed an agreement on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters, as leaders of both countries expect expanded relations in economy, information technology, defense as well as a strategic partnership amid security threats facing the two nations. President Marcos welcomed Polish President Karol Nawrocki and his delegation at Malacañang, where the latter was accorded arrival honors. This is the first visit of a head of state of the Republic of Poland to the Philippines. At a joint press conference at Malacañang, Marcos highlighted the two countries’ ongoing and future cooperation in key areas such as defense and security, trade, industry, agriculture, science and technology, information and communications technology, energy, legal cooperation and people-to-people relations. The President also cited the Philippines’ acquisition of S-70 Black Hawk combat utility helicopters from Poland as part of the modernization program of the Armed Forces of the Philippines. He said the two countries look forward to building on the outcomes of the inaugural Philippines-Poland Joint Defense Cooperation Committee, including through joint training and educational opportunities. Poland has been participating as an observer in the Balikatan Exercises since 2025. “President Nawrocki and I also had insightful exchange of views on regional and international matters of mutual concern, including the challenges in the South China Sea and security developments in Ukraine and in Europe,” Marcos said. “We reiterated our shared commitment to upholding the rule of law in international relations and the peaceful resolution of conflicts,” Marcos said. For his part, Nawrocki said defense cooperation is an important aspect of the two countries’ relations, as security challenges face by Europe and the Indo-Pacific “can no longer be approached separately.” “We want to develop this cooperation also in other areas,” the Polish leader said, noting that the IT sector is one of the important areas of potential cooperation between Warsaw and Manila. “We have discussed maritime security, state resilience, cyber security, also about the security of strategic supply chains,” Nawrocki said. “Today we want, and we are opening a new chapter in these relations. Poland is very much interested in raising our relationship to the level of a strategic partnership,” he noted. Marcos said he and Nawrocki reaffirmed the two countries’ respect for international law. “And of course, these incursions or attempts to change territorial definitions are unacceptable in both Poland and in the Philippines,” he said. Nawrocki will inaugurate today the fifth edition of the Polish-Filipino Economic IT Summit in Manila. He also asked the Philippines’ support for Poland’s permanent membership in the G20, as it is the 20th largest economy in the world, and has invited Marcos to visit Warsaw. The two countries signed the Agreement on a Transfer of Sentenced Persons earlier this year. Manila and Warsaw also affirmed their readiness to commence negotiations on an extradition agreement, Marcos said.
